title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: After midnight Banquo, unable to sleep, tells Fleance of 'cursed thoughts' and gives Macbeth a diamond from the king for Lady Macbeth. Banquo mentions dreaming of the Witches; Macbeth claims he does not think of them and hints at future honor if Banquo will 'cleave to my consent'; Banquo agrees only if he keeps his allegiance clear. Alone, Macbeth sees a dagger in the air leading him to Duncan, wonders if it is 'a dagger of the mind', and goes when the bell rings: 'Hear it not, Duncan; for it is a knell.'

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act II, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show the dagger of the mind? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act II, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the dagger of the mind? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act II, Scene I develops the idea of the dagger of the mind. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act II, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of the dagger of the mind. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act II, Scene I suggests about the dagger of the mind. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's imagery and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses imagery in Act II, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of the dagger of the mind. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act II, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the dagger of the mind responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act II, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the dagger of the mind follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act II, Scene I and its treatment of the dagger of the mind. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's imagery and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act II, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about the dagger of the mind in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act II, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the dagger of the mind. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Have you ever been so anxious or guilty that you imagined something that was not there? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are dudgeon, allegiance, husbandry, palpable, augment. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest; I see thee still,
And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood,
Which was not so before.” In this sentence it means: the handle of a dagger. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Macbeth would have known. Plays at the Globe were performed in daylight, so night had to be created by words: references to darkness, torches and the bell signal the hour. Why does this scene matter? The dagger soliloquy dramatizes a mind dividing against itself; whether the dagger is supernatural or hallucinated is left open, a pattern the play repeats with Banquo's ghost. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Hold, take my sword.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the dagger of the mind? I circle “husbandry”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find imagery, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Act II, Scene I develops the idea of the dagger of the mind. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to ambition and its costs? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the scene quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this scene suggests about the dagger of the mind, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how imagery shapes the dagger of the mind. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
